claims.text: CMS suggests comparing your bill with your EOB, both the services and the amount you owe, and paying only after you’ve checked that they match.

sources.title: How to read your medical bill

claims.text: For questions about a bill, or an error on your bill or EOB, CMS says to contact your provider or facility.

sources.title: How to read your medical bill

flags.title: This charge isn’t on the EOB you added
flags.detail: We couldn’t find a matching service on this EOB. It may be on a different EOB (plans often send one per provider or per visit), or the provider may not have sent it to your plan.

claims.text: If you don’t get an EOB for a service, CMS suggests asking your health plan whether the provider sent them a claim for it.

sources.title: How to read your medical bill

flags.title: The bill asks for more than the EOB says you owe
flags.detail: The bill says you owe $409.00. The EOB says you owe $367.00, a difference of $42.00. Part of the difference may be the charges that aren’t on this EOB.

claims.text: CMS says your bill should not be higher than the amount your EOB says you owe (the patient balance). If it is, talk to your provider.

sources.title: How to read a health insurance explanation of benefits
Check your medical bill for errors

claims.text: HealthCare.gov says a preferred (in-network) provider may not balance bill you for covered services, meaning bill you for the difference between its charge and the plan’s allowed amount.

flags.title: Your plan didn’t pay for this service
flags.detail: The EOB marks this line as denied or not covered. If you disagree with that decision, you may be able to appeal. The Denial Navigator can walk you through a denial notice.

flags.title: If this was emergency care, or care at an in-network hospital or surgery center
flags.detail: Federal and New Jersey surprise-billing protections may limit what you can be asked to pay. Whether they apply depends on your plan and where you got care.

claims.text: Under the federal No Surprises Act, if your plan covers emergency care, you generally can’t be charged more for emergency services than your in-network cost-sharing (copayment, deductible or coinsurance). Some protections depend on the setting and can be waived by signing a consent form for some non-emergency care.

sources.title: Know your rights when using insurance (No Surprises Act)

claims.text: For plans regulated in New Jersey, NJ DOBI says providers can’t bill you above your in-network cost-sharing for emergency or urgent care, or for inadvertent out-of-network care at an in-network facility (P.L.2018, c.32). Report such a bill to your insurer.

sources.title: Out-of-network Consumer Protection, Transparency, Cost Containment, and Accountability Act
sources.authority: New Jersey Department of Banking and Insurance

claims.text: For questions or complaints about surprise bills, the federal No Surprises Help Desk is 1-800-985-3059.

sources.title: Know your rights when using insurance (No Surprises Act)

comparison.disclaimer: These are differences worth asking about, not findings that anything is wrong. A bill and an EOB can differ for ordinary reasons, such as a payment you already made or a service on a separate EOB. Medicom doesn't decide whether a bill is correct; your provider and your plan can explain each line.
